conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for making time for this today. I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and help you feel supported as you settle into life with your new baby.  

The short questionnaire we’ll use is called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a well-tested set of 10 questions that helps us spot how mood and anxiety might be showing up for new moms in the first weeks and months after birth. Anything you share is confidential, and there’s no right or wrong answer—only what’s true for you. We’ll go at your pace; each question asks how you’ve felt in the past seven days, and I’ll re-phrase things conversationally so it feels less like a quiz and more like a chat.  

Ready to begin?  

1) Thinking about the past week: have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?
Honestly… I’ve had a couple moments where I smiled—like when my husband made that silly face at the baby—but they feel kind of forced. Mostly I just feel too tired and heavy to laugh.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
No… I can’t really say that. Nothing feels funny right now, and when people make jokes I just fake a little smile so they’ll stop asking.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I used to get excited about little stuff—my morning coffee, a walk, even folding tiny onesies—but now it all feels flat. I still do those things, mostly because I think I “should,” but the spark just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. If the baby fusses for more than a few minutes I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—like I’m already failing him as a mom. Rationally I know babies cry, but the guilt just jumps in before I can stop it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all the time. Even when everything looks fine—he’s breathing, he’s fed, he’s asleep—I still feel this knot in my chest. I’ll suddenly picture him spitting up and choking, or the blanket somehow covering his face, and then I can’t settle until I’ve checked the monitor three more times.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It’s like a sudden wave—my heart races, I feel shaky, and I have to remind myself to breathe. Nothing specific triggered it; it just hits out of nowhere, especially when the house gets quiet and I’m alone with the baby.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. I’ll be feeding the baby and notice the dishes piling up, and suddenly it feels like I’m drowning—like I’ll never catch up. I usually push through, but it’s exhausting, and some nights I cry after I finally get him down because it all feels like too much.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie there wired, running through everything I might’ve done wrong or imagining awful “what-ifs” about the baby. Some nights it takes me over an hour to fall asleep, and then I jolt awake at every little sound, heart pounding.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah... that pretty much sums up most of my days. It's not sobbing-all-day sad, but this gray cloud that won't lift. Everything feels heavy, and some mornings I open my eyes and already feel disappointed that it's a new day.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

A couple of times this week. It’s usually when I’m alone—like yesterday when I couldn’t get him to settle and I just sat in the rocker with tears running down my face. I felt so useless, like he deserves a better mom.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yeah… it’s popped into my head once or twice, just a fleeting “what if I weren’t here” kind of thought when everything feels too heavy. I’ve never planned anything and I don’t want to leave my baby, but the idea sneaks in for a second before I shove it away.

You've shared that the past weeks have felt overwhelmingly heavy-laughter rarely comes, simple pleasures like coffee or a walk now feel flat, and a constant knot of worry keeps you checking the monitor over and over. You cry easily, blame yourself whenever the baby fusses, and end most days exhausted yet wired, with fleeting scary thoughts that you might be better off gone. These feelings are understandably frightening, especially when you're trying so hard to be the mom your baby deserves.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports complete inability to find anything funny and feels compelled to fake smiles, matching 'Not at all</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of enjoyment in previously pleasurable activities, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame that is immediate and automatic, consistent with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports constant, intrusive worries and physical anxiety symptoms, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden panic episodes with physical symptoms that occur "sometimes," aligning with the "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed "most days," describes an inability to keep up with tasks, and ends most nights in tears—clearly matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption, racing thoughts, and hyper-arousal consistent with "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive low mood that colors most days and begins upon waking, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS of 25 falls well above the ≥14 high-risk cutoff; item 10 scored 1 indicating <sym>fleeting self-harm ideation</sym>. She describes most-days low mood, loss of interest, guilt, impaired sleep, tearfulness, and functional overwhelm starting after delivery, meeting core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and co-occurring <med>anxiety features</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day review with your <med>OB/midwife</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med>
2. Ask a trusted adult to stay with you and monitor for worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm
3. Call the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline 1-833-943-5746 or 988 if thoughts of harm intensify
4. Begin gentle daily routine: 15 min outdoor light walk, balanced meals, hydrate, accept help with night feeds to protect 4-hour sleep blocks
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress after treatment starts
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant <12 mo) – self-report

Date: [today]

Affect/ Mood: Persistent sad, “gray,” anhedonia; laughs only feigned; enjoyment absent from previously pleasurable daily tasks.  
Cognition: Pronounced guilt (“failing as mom”), worthlessness, catastrophic “what-ifs,” concentration intact but preoccupied.  
Anxiety: Near-continuous worry, no specific trigger; panic spells (racing heart, shakes) several times/week; hypervigilant re infant safety.  
Functional Impact: Feels “drowning,” tasks overwhelming; frequent crying; sleep initiation impaired by rumination; multiple nocturnal awakenings.  
Safety: Fleeting passive suicidal thoughts (“what if I weren’t here”) without plan or intent; denies desire to leave baby; no self-harm behaviors reported.  

Pattern: Symptoms present most days for recent weeks; onset after delivery; consistent with probable major depressive episode with anxious distress in postpartum context.

Risk flags  
– Passive SI with hopelessness  
– Significant impairment in self-care and infant-care confidence  
– Anxiety intensity interfering with rest

Screening conclusion: High likelihood of clinically significant postpartum depression ± anxiety; safety risk present. Recommend immediate comprehensive evaluation by perinatal mental health specialist and safety-planning.
